messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Curriculum Designer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 33

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the therapy office with his shoulders drawn inward, fingers picking at a loose thread on his jeans. At thirty, he carries himself with the careful deliberation of someone who has learned to make himself smaller. He's a curriculum designer for an educational nonprofit, work he describes as "meaningful," though his voice flattens when he says it—as though meaning itself has become difficult to access.

Two years ago, Marcus was in a relationship with David. They had been together for three years, and by most external measures, it looked good. They traveled together, attended gallery openings, talked about a future. What Marcus didn't tell anyone was how the relationship had gradually shifted. The criticism came first—subtle observations about his appearance, his career choices, the way he spent time with friends. David was charming about it, framing everything as concern. Marcus found himself second-guessing his own perceptions.

The physical violence began on a Thursday evening after Marcus mentioned attending a work conference in another city. David was drinking. Marcus remembers the shock of it more than the pain—David's hand across his face, the force of it unexpected, almost unreal. When Marcus tried to leave the apartment, David blocked the door. The evening fractured into fragments in Marcus's memory: raised voices, his own body pressed against the wall, David's hands around his wrists, the specific smell of David's cologne mixed with alcohol.

Afterward, David cried. He apologized profusely, called it a one-time mistake, blamed stress and alcohol. Marcus believed him because he needed to believe him. But it happened again six weeks later, and then again. Each time followed a similar pattern—David's remorse, his promises, Marcus's hope that things would change. When Marcus finally left, it took him three months to actually go.

Now, two years later, Marcus still startles at unexpected touches. A colleague placing a hand on his shoulder during a meeting sends adrenaline through his system. He finds himself unable to focus during curriculum meetings, his mind suddenly elsewhere, replaying conversations searching for signs he missed. He's become hyperaware of people's tone of voice, interpreting neutral comments as criticism or threat.

Dating feels impossible. He's tried twice since the breakup, but when things begin to feel intimate, panic rises in his chest. His body remembers what his mind tries to minimize. He's downloaded dating apps and deleted them. He tells himself he's simply not ready, which is true, but there's something deeper—a fundamental distrust of his own judgment that he can't shake.

His work has suffered too. Marcus prides himself on his creativity and attention to detail, but lately he finds himself staring at curriculum frameworks without absorbing them. He's missed deadlines, something that never happened before. His supervisor has been kind about it, but Marcus feels the weight of his own decline. He used to stay late, enthusiastically tweaking lesson plans. Now he leaves at five o'clock, goes home to his quiet apartment, and scrolls through his phone until sleep comes.

What troubles Marcus most is the anger that surfaces unexpectedly. He'll be designing a unit on resilience for high school students, and something about the language will trigger fury so intense it frightens him. He's snapped at friends who didn't deserve it. He's had moments of rage toward David that feel disproportionate, even though he knows they're not. The anger coexists with shame—shame that he stayed, shame that he didn't see it coming, shame that he still sometimes wonders if he overreacted.

He doesn't think of himself as traumatized. That word feels too big, too dramatic for what happened. But something is broken in how he moves through the world now, and he's not sure how to repair it.
